utterances.text: Madam Registrar -- Mr. Registrar, good morning to you. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forgive my mistaken identity, but after International Women's Day, you wouldn't blame me. So, all the accused are here. All the Defence teams are in full force today. utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the position of the Defence teams on this? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Mr. President, the -- our initial view on -- with respect to these documents, and I'm talking about documents P2231 to P2234, our initial position was to object from the get-go before this witness would testify, because they did not have Rule 65 ter numbers. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Any further comments from the Defence teams? None. Do you want -- wish to respond to that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So I think basically your response, in part, at least, means that the Prosecution can be exempted from filing an ad hoc motion. Is that correct, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That is indeed correct, Mr. President. And I forgot to mention one thing is, of course, based on what my colleague said yesterday concerning the second -- I'm looking at the exhibits from 2233 and 2234 where my colleague said that he did not intend to lead any evidence from these documents with respect to the acts and conduct of the -- of any of the accused, I invite the Trial Chamber to basically maybe not taken -- not admit these two documents. But it's not an objection on our part. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you wish to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I do think they have information in it that may be helpful to the Court in looking at the overall product of this witness, and they were part of the record of the last case upon which the 92 bis statement was based. So I think it would be a good idea for the Court to have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. One further thing in relation to a statement that you made yesterday at the beginning of the sitting, Mr. McCloskey. When you referred to the tactical intercepts notebook at the beginning of the sitting, actually, I can go straight to it. You said that in relation to tactical intercepts notebook you were not tendering that if -- in as far as it may contain references to the acts and conducts of any of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the -- what I meant to say was we had a notebook, this little hard-back notebook and that's what Mr. Haynes and I spent most of the time talking about. That does have acts or conducts material for Vinko Pandurevic, and that is offered for his acts and conduct. The pile of papers from the second site is the one I was referring to that I am not asking for any acts of conduct evidence in those piles of papers. There is a couple of references that sound familiar, but I don't think it was necessary to -- to use that evidence in that manner, or go to the effort of calling witnesses, and all that would be part of that. So that pile of paper I could ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But which one --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll get you the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We want -- we would like to know whether it is P02231 or P02232, because in the list that we have they are both described as tactical intercept notebooks. The first one, dates covered are 1st July to 24th November of 1995. The second one the same. But the second one is draft English translation. So I would imagine that you are referring to both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- 2233 and 2234 are the stack of papers from the second site, English and B/C/S. And that's what I refer to when I say no acts or conducts evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are referring to P02233, so with reference to yesterday's statement by Mr. McCloskey as per page -- as contained in page 6, line 7, to page 7, line 5 of the transcript, reference was to Exhibit P02233, and its translation -- equivalent translation in English, P02234. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. Those are the papers from site two that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then in the second part of your statement yesterday you said, "As for the notebook for the other material, that principally --" one moment. "That principally goes to the acts or conducts of General Pandurevic, which Mr. Haynes and I will be debating, perhaps some issues, but you will see how that falls out. But that's just the background of -- I'm not aware of any other acts or conduct from that material of any other accused though there are code-names that I am not aware of who they are, but for your knowledge the notebook will go to acts and conducts of General Pandurevic." Could you specify exactly which tactical notebook you are now referring to? Or you were then referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is 2232 and 2231, and of course in the -- the recent motion we will be filing we will set out the relevance of the particular parts that we're referring to. So that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Haynes, do you agree with -- not with its substance or its validity, but its -- the correctness of the reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree that 2231 and 2232 are the relevant notebooks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. So are there any other objections on the part of the Defence, of any of the Defence teams in relation to the other exhibits that the Prosecution wishes to tender? Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Not an objection, but while it's fresh in our minds, I put certain figures to the witness yesterday, which had been the subject of discussions between myself and Mr. McCloskey. In fact, he corrected me on one of them. We did agree that, I think, Lovac appears in that notebook 82 times; Lovac 1, 62 times; Parma, 11 times; and Pavle, now, seven times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were he correcting you -- corrected you whether it was three times or four times on that particular page, but that's not material. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We will agree to that, though, as we all know, we may be off a number or two. But yes, that's a credible counting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you also agree that these tactical intercept notebooks should, like other intercepts, be for the time being marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would, unless Defence counsel would like to jump that particular hurdle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't imagine so, but Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Perhaps safer that we take the course you suggest for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any further objections or remarks or statements in relation to the exhibits that the Prosecution wishes to tender? None. So those marked in bold characters will remain under seal. Intercepts will be marked for identification purposes, and as -- as far as P02233, P02234, with the caveat that I referred to earlier on, namely that they are not to constitute evidence of -- they are not to go to the acts or conducts of any of the accused, or they are not meant to be. The rest are admitted, but, please, Mr. Registrar, I would like you to consult with the participants; any one of them should remain under seal. Okay. Does any one of the Defence team wish to tender any documents? We hear none. We hear none. So that chapter is closed, and we can move to the ruling that we promised you yesterday and which we couldn't hand down in time. As the issues that we will be dealing with are interrelated, we thought we would best address them together. The first relates to the objection which was raised during the sitting of two days ago in relation to the admission of the document which was attached to the witness statement, namely the attendance sheet bearing ERN 0606-6236. Two issues were raised which I will address in reverse order. It was suggested that the fact that this document was created by another person precluded its admission into evidence through yesterday's -- or through Witness PW-158. We disagree. The witness was able to identify and describe the document, and the witness gave evidence as to how he obtained it. It was indeed used in his testimony. It is clearly relevant, and the fact that he is not the author of the document does not, in this Tribunal, preclude its admission. I need not remind anyone of the vast array of documents which are before us, including many submitted by the Defence that have been introduced through witnesses who did not create them. The second argument raises -- raised -- the second argument raised relates to the 65 ter list, on which we have heard several submissions during the past months. Let us make it clear: We do attach importance to Rule 65 ter, as expressed in our previous decisions, but we also take a purposeful and pragmatic approach to it. While generally the Prosecution should be applying to amend its list when it intends to use new documents with a particular witness, as circumstances will vary from case to case, this is not an absolute requirement. In the case of this particular entry from the logbook, namely the attendance sheet to which I referred earlier on, this is a document that the witness produced after having first obtained it from a colleague. The document was of use to the witness in confirming the dates of his shifts in January of 1995. When such a document is produced to the Prosecution, what is important is that it be disclosed to the Defence in a timely manner. In this case we believe that was done. The only remaining issue then was whether the Defence felt they were in a position to proceed with cross-examination, given the recent nature of the disclosure. Since the Defence confirmed that they were, and indeed there was extensive cross-examination carried out with respect to the log, we do not see this submission as a ground for not admitting the document in evidence. However, we believe that the proper procedure in instances like this is for the Prosecution to tender the document as a separate exhibit, with its own number, rather than incorporating it as part of a statement. This will avoid any problems in locating and identifying the document in future. This document is therefore being admitted, but as a separate exhibit. We now move to an issue raised earlier on during the week. Again, with respect to the 65 ter list. This time in the context of a redirect of witness, Ms. Stefanie Frease conducted by the Prosecution on the 6th of March. Rule 65 ter is designed to provide for disclosure of documents and exhibits the Prosecution intends to call or offer, respectively. The original list is filed at the pre-trial stage, and, as such, it relates directly to the Prosecution's intention at that time. Obviously the Prosecution, in preparing this list, cannot be expected to anticipate the content and direction of every cross-examination so as to be in a position to also include any document that might possibly be needed for redirect. Material identified for use in redirect need not be included in the 65 ter list, or be given a 65 ter number before it is made use of. Needless to say, this procedure would equally be applicable to the Defence at the appropriate time. Similarly, the Defence contends that the Prosecution has to identify such documents as part of the list of exhibits intended to be used with the witness, which list is tendered prior to examination-in-chief. Again, the Prosecution cannot be expected to list any document that it thinks might possibly be needed for redirect. This would actually serve to confuse, rather than clarify matters, as the exhibit list for each witness would be cluttered with material which might never, in reality, then be introduced by the Prosecution. As a result, the documents at issue, namely P02438, P02467 and P02469 were properly put to the witness in redirect, and they are accordingly admitted. So I think we can now move. Are there any other -- one moment, because I have a problem with my ... Are there any preliminaries that you would like to raise? Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We take good note and we thank the Chamber for its ruling on these issues which we believe indeed are important. That being said, there are two issues I would like to raise concerning the date book which was just admitted. First of all what is admitted is only two pages of the date book and not the complete date book, which is the first preliminary issue. I would like, Mr. President, because your ruling says that this Trial Chamber believes that this exhibit was disclosed to the Defence in time. I would like the Prosecution to confirm - I have spoken to my colleague - that document had not been given to us until the morning before cross-examination began. So if we can get my colleague to confirm this, and I have shown him the memorandum which was sent us saying that that document would be disclosed to us, but it was never. It was included on the electronic court system, but never sent, nor given to us. That's the first issue. The second issue, Mr. President, concerning the -- this date book, and now I'm referring to the complete date book. I asked yesterday before this Trial Chamber that we would like to have the complete date book disclosed to us, and my colleague from the Prosecution responded that he was about to -- he was trying to get a copy of it before it moved out. We believe it is important indeed that a copy be made out before the witness leaves with this date book because of the issues that were raised in cross-examination, namely the fact that some pages were taken away from the book. So we would not like to lose or that -- to have this item of evidence, of potentially evidence to move out without a copy being made and disclosed to the Defence so that we may consider whether it would be necessary to recall, for further cross-examination, the owner of the document. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, you have repeated what you have said yesterday. What's the latest on the commitment that you made yesterday, Mr. McCloskey, to try and make sure it remains here and be disclosed in its entirety to the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We did capture it, and -- last night, and it was to be scanned, either this morning or last night. And so we have it, and it's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What -- is there a problem in keeping it here, available in case further questions are asked in relation to the missing pages, or as it has been put, torn pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think so. We were going to contact its owner and -- and find out. But I don't think so, given what's happened and the attitude that the witnesses have all shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. As regards the first point that was raised by Mr. Bourgon, I don't think there is any further comments from your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, if there is any help needed on when these materials were provided counsel, we can give that. But of course it is our view that when something is identified clearly and it's in an electronic record, accessible to the Defence -- I don't know if you want me to get into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't think we are on the same wave-length. It's -- the submission that Mr. Bourgon made it was not disclosed in a timely fashion because it was disclosed the day -- same day as the hearing. I was under the impression that since it formed part of the witness's statement at time, one of you, I think it was Mr. Vanderpuye, had stated that it had been disclosed quite a few days earlier, as part of the statement, and that there -- it was therefore available to the Defence teams when the statement itself was disclosed. I mean I start corrected if that is not the correct position, perhaps you can enlighten us on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, think you're correct, but Mr. Vanderpuye knows the details of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you wish to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Perhaps I can clarify a couple of things. My recollection, although it is foggy, and it shouldn't be, is that the witness in question testified, I think, on the 7th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Prior to that, on the 28th of February, which is I think a day after the statement itself was signed, notification of the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 27th of February it was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Right. 27th of February. Notification of the statement was sent to the Defence. In the context of that notification we specifically referred to the documents that were shown to the witness and noted that one document was attached to his statement and that the other documents had been loaded into e-court. Mr. Bourgon is correct that the physical page wasn't sent to the Defence, but it was part of the electronic submission of what had been uploaded into e-court and I think the Defence's attention was drawn to that fact in the 28th February e-mail or communication that we had with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can leave it at that. It is our -- Mr. Bourgon, I don't think there is need for further submissions. We are going to close it there. We take note of what you submitted. Our ruling is to enjoin the Prosecution to do its level best to disclose all material in a timely fashion to the Defence teams. Otherwise, we will encounter problems, otherwise we will be put in a position where we have to postpone cross-examinations, where possibly we may even have to postpone sittings. So please do your level best. I know that we are pressurising you to move, and move, and move, but that shouldn't mean that certain principles can be dispensed with. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I need to say for the record that I do not have that correspondence with me today, but I will produce that e-mail simply to say that to the best of my recollection, there were no references of this material being placed on e-court. Had there been such a reference, we would have went to go and get the document on e-court. In this case, my recollection said that this material will be -- will be provided to you as soon as practically possible. The material was not provided to us. When we received a copy of that statement initially on 28th February, it was a draft version with actually track changes. The final copy of the statement we only took it on the morning of the testimony of the witness, and that's when we can see this document for the first time. Was it our responsibility to go and get this document or is it the responsibility of the Prosecution to give us that document in advance, especially that it is a new document that does not have a 65 ter number, that was not on their list, and that was produced by -- specifically for this witness. We believe, Mr. President, it was the duty of the Prosecution to give us this document, which was only give to us on the morning. And the morning of the testimony I went to see my colleague and I asked him, "Where is this date report?" And that's when he showed me the statement that had been uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think -- let's close it here. If there is a filing from Mr. Bourgon, please feel free to answer it or to file whatever you feel like. But I think we shouldn't take more of our court time. Let's bring in the next witness, please. I just want to make sure, because I was checking yesterday, that this witness did not have any protective measures in the previous trials where he testified. Does he have protective measures or are you seeking protective measures for him for this case or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. You're correct. No protective measures before, no protective measures now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: However, out of an abundance of caution and my friends might suggest it, I told the witness that -- exactly, that it was likely that that would occur and he anticipates that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has the provision of our Rules been explained to him or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've explained it to him as best I could, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That should be -- so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are a Prosecution witness. Before you start your testimony you need to undertake in a solemn way that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher is going to be giving you the text of the solemn declaration that you are required to make. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. You will be examined in chief by Mr. Nicholls, whom you've met already. He will then be followed by several of the Defence teams on cross-examination. You lived part of the events that are part of the subject matter of this case, or so is the suggestion. It is my responsibility on behalf of the Trial Chamber to bring to your attention a provision which we have in our Rules which is included out of due deference to a principle that no one should be expected to incriminate himself. I'm referring to the possibility that in the course of your testimony questions may be put to you which, if answered, could possibly, in your mind, incriminate you. You have a protection against that in our Rules, which provide that a witness may object to answering a question or making a statement which might tend to incriminate him. However, this is not an absolute rule. It's not an absolute right that you have. We may, after deliberating, decide to exempt you from answering such questions, or we may decide to compel you to answer such questions. If we compel you to answer such questions, you are covered because any testimony that you might give when you are compelled to give it shall not be used as evidence in any subsequent prosecution which might be taken against you, except if we catch you giving false testimony. In that case, if your statement amounts to false testimony, then it can be used against you. So is it clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand this has already been explained to you. I just want to make sure that you understand your rights.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we can safely proceed now. Mr. Nicholls, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As I explained, it to you, I tried to, it's going to be a little different, your testimony. We are going to submit a transcript and so there will not be as many questions from me to you and I will read a summary of your testimony. First of all, let me ask you this: With the assistance of an interpreter who read it to you, did you review the entire transcript of your testimony, your prior testimony in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: It was more in the Jokic case than Blagojevic case, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You read your entire -- you had your entire prior testimony read to you though. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you please attest that the transcript of that testimony accurately reflects, to the best of your memory, what you stated during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The essence of the events, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, if you could start with identification of the witness. Name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And your name, sir, is Pero Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One last question on the transcript. Could you also confirm that if you were asked the same questions again today that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Before I read the summary, Your Honours, I would like to just run through the exhibits that were used before and their current numbers to make it easier when reviewing the transcript. In the previous testimony the witness was shown P525, which is 65 ter number 82 in this case. He was also shown P229, which has two 65 ter numbers in this case, 997 and 1161. He was shown a photograph, P17.2, which in this case is 1773 and 1774. It's the same photograph, it's just that in the prior exhibit it was put together as a panoramic. So 77 -- 1773 is the left part of P17.2 and 1774 is the right part of P17.2. He was shown photograph P19.3, which is 1811 in this case. Finally, Your Honours, there were two exhibits shown in the prior testimony, which we applied for and you granted the motion, I thank you, to allow us to add that to our 65 ter list. That was P666, a diagram drawn by the witness, which now has number 02471, and P667, a map which now has 65 ter number 02472. That is all of the exhibits which will be included, and I will now read a short summary of the prior testimony. Mr. Petrovic was born on the 8th of March, 1960 in Gornja Pilica Zvornik municipality. He is a Bosnian Serb. Presently Mr. Petrovic works as an assistant warehouse keeper at the Birac company in Zvornik. In May 1992 he was mobilised into the VRS and served as a soldier in the 1st Infantry Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. At this time he also held the position of the president of the Pilica local commune. The Pilica local commune is an organ which represents the needs of the local population before the official organs of Zvornik municipality. The witness testified that the main purpose of the local commune is to ensure that the basic infrastructure is maintained and that basic services are provided for the residents of the commune. During the war Mr. Petrovic spent the majority of his time in his duties as president of the Pilica local commune, rather than with his duties as a soldier in the Zvornik Brigade. However, to be clear, all the time from his mobilisation in 1992 until demobilisation in March 1996, Mr. Petrovic was a soldier of the Zvornik Brigade. Moving on now to the core of his testimony. In July 1995 Mr. Petrovic still held his position as president of the local commune. Around St. Peter's day, 12 July 1995, he was at home in Pilica on leave. On a day around St. Peter's day Mr. Petrovic met a woman near the Kula school in Pilica. The woman approached him and told him that she had been told that if possible all the children in homes near the school should be moved away because prisoners would be brought there, and that children should not look at that and shouldn't gather around the school. Mr. Petrovic then spoke with a soldier a little bit further down the road, still near the Pilica school. Mr. Petrovic knew this soldier personally. And his name was Slavko Peric. Slavko Peric was a member of the 1st Infantry Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. This was around 10 or 11.00 a.m., approximately. Mr. Petrovic asked Mr. Peric if he knew what was going on. Peric told Mr. Petrovic that the battalion command, his battalion command had just received a telegram and that the premises should be made ready to receive prisoners, that the premises should be prepared. Mr. Petrovic understood this to mean the premises of the school -- Kula school, as that was the only facility there which would accommodate prisoners. Mr. Petrovic asked Slavko Peric who had signed this telegram and Peric responded that he did not know. After this conversation Mr. Petrovic proceeded to his office, located at Pilica Dom. Shortly thereafter he met some local villagers who also asked him to find out what was going on around the school. The telephone lines were temporarily down at this time, so Mr. Petrovic decided to go to Sepak to make a call from the home of Jovo Ivanovic. Jovo Ivanovic was an SDS member, and in his testimony Mr. Petrovic did not recall precisely what his working position was in July of 1995. And at Jovo Ivanovic's house the witness used the telephone to call the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade. Mr. Petrovic then spoke directly with the Zvornik Brigade duty officer at the time, Dragan Jokic. Mr. Petrovic personally knew Dragan Jokic from work they had done together in 1992 and 1993, when Dragan Jokic and his unit had built roads in the Pilica commune. Mr. Petrovic testified that he had a high opinion of Dragan Jokic. During this telephone call Dragan Jokic introduced himself by saying, "This is Dragan Jokic." Stated that he was the duty officer, and Mr. Petrovic also recognised his voice. The conversation they had was brief. The witness asked Jokic what was going on in Pilica and whether it was true that the prisoners were coming. Dragan Jokic told Mr. Petrovic that this was none of his concern and that he should mind his own business. Again, Mr. Petrovic is not sure of the exact date of this conversation, but knows and testified that it was sometime around St. Peter's day, meaning the 12th of July, 1995. Mr. Petrovic then returned to Pilica with some villagers who had brought him to Sepak. They discussed what to do and ultimately decided that there was nothing they could do, and that the question of prisoners being brought to the Kula school in Pilica was out of their hands. After returning from Sepak Mr. Petrovic passed the Kula school in Pilica and saw about 20 buses parked by the school. There were prisoners on the buses. Soldiers were guarding the prisoners. The soldiers stood in front of and around the buses. Mr. Petrovic assumed that these prisoners were from Srebrenica. He went home for a little while and then left to walk towards his office in the Dom. At the Kula school, as he passed by, he saw that the prisoners were there still, and he spent about 30 minutes at the school. He could hear voices in the school corridors, though the prisoners remained on the buses while Mr. Petrovic was present. He then proceeded to his office. The following day Mr. Petrovic went to Zvornik on business. On the way back from Zvornik, around the area of the Kiseljacki road, he noticed a column of five to six buses headed in the direction of Zvornik. Mr. Petrovic testified he assumed these were prisoners from the Kula school being transferred and he testified that the location was approximately where the Kozluk-Padine road forks off towards Kiseljak. On his return from Zvornik Mr. Petrovic went to the Dom in Pilica where his office is. Sometime before evening fell a VRS soldier came and asked him for the key for the big community hall in the Dom. And the community hall, as he testified, is directly behind his office. This soldier told Mr. Petrovic to unlock the hall so the prisoners could be put there. Mr. Petrovic told the soldier he did not have the key, it was then in the possession of an employee or employees of Agroprom. The soldier then asked for a wrench or a hammer so that he could open the door anyway, and Mr. Petrovic told him that he did not have one. Soon he saw buses full of men arriving at the Dom. The buses parked on the Dom-Kosa road, and the prisoners began to disembark and went towards the hall. Mr. Petrovic then left and went to a restaurant across the road from the Dom. At the restaurant he asked the owner to go and buy some bread for the prisoners. He then went to another restaurant and again asked this owner to procure bread for the prisoners. Mr. Petrovic went to his office and later bread was brought to the Dom and he asked one of the guards to give the bread to the prisoners. Mr. Petrovic then went back to the restaurant and then began to go home. He was tired and a local policeman saw him and said you should go home. Mr. Petrovic told the policeman he did not want to walk by the Kula school, and the policeman stopped a passing car and told the driver to give Mr. Petrovic a ride home by a different route. Mr. Petrovic stayed home for the next two days, coming back to his in the Dom on Monday morning, so the Monday after St. Peter's day. At the Dom, directly in front of the community hall, he saw a truck with soldiers standing around it. The soldiers were loading the corpses of people who had been killed into the truck. A few days later Mr. Petrovic heard local people saying that these corpses were buried at the Branjevo farm. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just going to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Witness, you've heard my summary. Is it correct to the best -- as you recall, of what's contained in your transcript?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those events and that's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No questions at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I pass him to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Nicholls. I have on my list the Popovic team. Go ahead, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's clarify something that my learned friend already asked you about. You just said to us that you saw, by the school in Kula, about 20 buses with people on them who use supposed were from Srebrenica. And then you said that you went home after that and that upon your return you saw again some buses and some people on the buses. I understood it to be that upon your return you heard that there were already some prisoners in the school. In other words, that in the meantime, while you were gone, some people had been taken off buses and put in the school?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: On my return from home to the school I heard voices in the school. That's what it was. And it's true that I saw the buses parked in front of the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My second question is this: On the following day you went to Zvornik, among other places?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that upon your return you saw five to six buses going from Pilica in the direction of Zvornik. You said to my learned friend that this was the intersection going from Kozluk to Padine and so on. I wanted to remind you of your previous testimony in the Blagojevic and Jokic case, where a map was shown to you. You pointed out the village of Rocevici on that map. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the village of Rocevici was on the map, and before that village, in the direction of Kiseljak there was a village of Padine and in my mind, Padine is linked to Rocevici. This two places are linked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate you saw this convoy of five to six buses near Rocevici?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. After Rocevici on the way to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But on the map you showed Rocevici?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, when asked where Rocevici was, I pointed out where Rocevici was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, those of us following the proceedings in English can feel the stress in the interpreter's voice in trying to catch up with you. Witness and Mr. Zivanovic, please allow a pause between question and answer, allowing the interpreters to translate to us in English and French, otherwise there will be stuff missing in the transcript, and that's not fair. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will just switch to English channel to avoid this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw -- well, yes, in fact you did show this, but I will not go into that. On that occasion you also said that the -- that there had been people on the buses that you had seen people on those buses in the five or six buses, let me be quite clear?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: It was quite unusual for me to see this convoy of vehicles, and I felt that if they were heading to Zvornik I had this idea in my mind that these people were being taken from Pilica back to Zvornik, and I saw that there were people, but I wasn't able to tell who they were, but my idea was that these people who could not be put in Pilica were then taken back to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You concluded that on the bases of the similarity of the buses that were used for the other people that you saw up there, so the buses, the two sets of buses were similar?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. As far as I can remember they were quite similar. There were no major differences. I don't know what the colour was of those buses, red, yellow, blue, but they were similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, among other things, that you saw on that day, on one of those days, before those prisoners were brought in, that you saw Slavko Peric, a person by the name of Slavko Peric. Now, my question to you is, did you see this person later on while the prisoners were there in the school, so from the moment when the prisoners were brought in and later on?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: A couple of hours before they were brought in from Zvornik, I saw Slavko Peric and, since I did not really spend time around the school, I cannot remember. I mean, it is impossible for me to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him on the day when you saw the bodies being loaded?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more thing. In the transcript that I read, I saw that a good portion of that transcript was devoted to your correcting the statement that you had given to the Prosecution earlier. Four to five pages were devoted to this effort. You spoke in some detail about what was missing or what was incorrect in the statement that you had given. So you made quite a lot of corrections. Is my question to you is, before you testified, had you have the occasion to actually see this statement in B/C/S, that's what we call the Serbo-Croatian language here. So did you have occasion to read the statement in this language?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand, what corrections to what statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try and remind you. You testified before this Tribunal in December 2003. One year before that you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a statement, but this person was not introduced to me as a representative of the Prosecutor's office. I gave a statement, but this person did not specify that she is from the Office of the Prosecutor. This was an informal conversation, and some notes were taken by this person, and the corrections related to some elements in the -- in the translation, and some terms were used in the B/C/S language that I complained about, wrong word for "shop" was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you made quite a lot of corrections, four or five pages of the corrections?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't really think it's four or five pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you are moving too fast. After Mr. Zivanovic has finished putting his question, allow a short pause, and then you start giving your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, and I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, until the time when you came here to testify, you did not have the statement in its written form in Serbo Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Until I arrived here in The Hague, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We better make this clear. When you say "until the time when you came here to testify," you're referring to the previous time, not this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the previous testimony in 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how we took it, we just wanted a confirmation of that. Go ahead. No further questions, Mr. Zivanovic. I have on my list Defence team for Mr. -- Colonel Beara. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I have Ms. Nikolic for Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will ask you a couple of questions so I can understand better the events that you are testifying about. If I understand you correctly, in this period, in July 1995, you were the president of the local commune in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the same time you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the 1st Battalion in the logistics platoon. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1st Battalion, but logistics platoon, I'm not quite sure about that. This changed a lot. I would be in the 1st Company and then I would be put in the 2nd Company, then I would be in the guards detail, then logistics platoon. It would change, the commander would just put me where there was need for people. But at that time I was resubordinated to a unit that was at the Misic [phoen] plateau. So that was at the very front-line.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So you were a soldier throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I fought.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's reply was inaudible.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to what you testified in the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Because I have on my transcript, "the witness's reply was inaudible," but still we have the answer, "Yes, I fought." Did you say anything else apart from, "Yes, I fought"? The question that was put to you by Ms. Nikolic was, "So you were a soldier throughout this period." Then what we have in the transcript is, "Yes, I fought." Then I have the interpreter note, "the witness's reply was inaudible." Do you wish to add anything to your answer, "Yes, I fought"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In fact what I said was I was resubordinated to a unit that was deployed at the front-line at the Nisic plateau at the time of the events in Pilica, and before that I was supposed to go there yet I didn't. I was given leave not to go because of the situation in my family, and my brother, who was the commander in the unit, gave me a leave of absence, so I was at home in this period. But I -- according to my file, I was at this unit that was deployed at the Nisic plateau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would now like to go back to the events that you describe in your testimony in the Blagojevic and Jokic case that was summarised by my friend at the Prosecution. At the time when you met Mr. Peric, you telephoned and you went back, that's when you saw the buses in front of the school and you stayed there for maybe 30 minutes. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers around those buses, or, in fact, on the buses guarding the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Around the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you know these people?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I didn't know most of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that they were not from your battalion in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us move on to Monday. You spent, if I'm not mistaken, Friday, you spent Friday, Saturday and Sunday home, you did not pass through Pilica on those days?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Friday, Saturday, Sunday, until Monday, but it's possible that I was there on Friday. But Saturday and Sunday until Monday, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you have any phone calls, did anyone call you, anyone -- any of the locals to ask you what was going on?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mean at home?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a phone line installed in my home at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you came to work on Monday, and when you described the situation that you described in your statement, can you please tell me, do you know who took the people from the school, who executed them, and where they were executed?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I was not able to see the actual execution, and I didn't see the events around the school. So I cannot tell you that because I was at home at that time. So the very act, I have no knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No knowledge of it, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Nikolic. According to our records, the Borovcanin team --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have no questions for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for confirming that. Madam Fauveau for General Miletic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And according to our records also the Gvero Defence team doesn't wish to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. And we have an indication that the Pandurevic Defence team wishes to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You have mentioned that at the time of the events that have been described you were not, as it were, actively employed as a soldier because you were given compassionate leave. Is it also the case that you were permitted, from time to time, to avoid service as a soldier because of your job as chairman of the local commune?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: In that period I think that I never asked the commander of the Nisic plateau unit to take me to the unit, and I -- I felt quite comfortable, because he had allowed me to go, because the local battalion troops, as a rule, should not actually give me any orders. As I already said, I spent 90 per cent of my time in the local commune and only 10 per cent in -- in the ranks. But in 1992, 1993, 1994, and then in 1995, in fact, I couldn't say anymore that I spent more time in the local commune premises than in the army. In 1995 I would often go in the field with some other units. I was not in my original unit, and I was -- I had stronger links with the unit at that time. Because the battalion commander decided that I was needed there, and I would spend time in the local commune when I had some days off, or if there was any need, any immediate need for me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Another topic, please. Was it your understanding of the position that Pilica village was outside the zone of defence of the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, to my knowledge, to my understanding, the 1st Infantry Battalion did have its area of responsibility in Pilica because we were in the Zvornik area, which included Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Moving on. The two premises you have described, the Kula school and the Pilica cultural centre, were they buildings for which you, as chairman of the local commune, had responsibility?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. Well, the president of the local commune has no responsibility over buildings. The school has its principal, has the relevant institutions in charge of the school, and the president of the local commune can go into the school when he is invited by the responsible person; in this case, that would be the principal. As far as the cultural centre is concerned, it was property of Agroprom Zvornik; they had their management, they had their manager. As regards the local commune office, I knew at the time, and I know now that this was the property of the Zvornik municipality. On the basis of all this I can say here that the activities of the local commune, that, in fact, what we did was we tried to figure out who actually owned the cultural centre and I asked this question as the deputy in the Zvornik municipal assembly, I think it was in 1996, and the answer I got was that the cultural centre should be placed at the disposal of the local communes. Unfortunately the cultural centre in Pilica is now the subject of a legal suit between Agroprom and the municipality. But to cut a long story short, the local commune had no responsibility, was not in charge of the school or of the cultural centre except in -- it had nothing to do with the actual buildings, except when the local commune had the use of some buildings that actually belonged to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's leave the cultural centre to one side. But so far as the property of the local commune was concerned, municipal authority, if the army wished to use municipal property it would obtain a requisitioning order, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand your question. Because that has to do with the military system. I don't know how the military could obtain premises. I just don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, the point of the question is, if the army wished to use municipal property, such as the school, an order was served upon you, as the president of the local commune, saying that that property was requisitioned for the purposes of the army, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. No. The local battalion command would probably put in a request through its superior command for the premises; that would be the brigade command, and then the brigade command would have to talk to the municipality. But the local commune, you have to understand, had no power to give anyone to give anything to anyone regarding any premises. First of all, you would have to go to the school, to the principal, to ask for the use of the school, and in case of the cultural centre you would have to address the manager of Agroprom. So they had no call to talk to the local commune at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So if I understand the position, it would be the municipal authority that would receive an order requisitioning the school, rather than the local commune?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that that's how it should be. But I'm not sure whether the military would go directly to the school principal or to the municipality. I can't know that. I don't know what the military would do. All I know is that there was no need for them to talk to me or to the local commune regarding those premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. One last thing. You are aware of the existence of Branjevo Farm, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There are two enterprises at Branjevo Farm, one operated by the army, and the other operated by a private company. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you whether that is correct or not, but I do know that there was a farm there before the war. I think that the owners were from Nova Selo, that was a state-owned company. And during the war I think that Agroprom actually was in charge of this farm. They ran it. Not some private company. And the agreement was, this is what I learned, with Agroprom, to allow the military to do some things there to grow some vegetables for their needs. But this was not privately owned. I don't know where you get your information. Because at that time there were no privately owned businesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's probably my mistake, but Agroprom did not give over the whole farm to the military, did it?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know that. I don't know how much of the farm was given over to the army by Agroprom, but I know that some people went there to work, and they were in the army. But I assume that the army controlled some parts of this farm, and that this had, in fact, been handed over to the army by Agroprom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes the cross-examination. Mr. Nicholls, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, your testimony finishes here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber I would like to thank you for having come over to give evidence. Our staff will give you all the assistance you need to facilitate your return back home. And we all wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's a matter unrelated to the witness, just before the break, that I would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think the sheet has been distributed. None of them need to be under seal. They would be the same ones I read out at the beginning, plus the witness's 92 ter testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections on the part of any of the Defence teams? Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not see the list, so I can't really say. Can the Prosecutor provide us with a list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hasn't the list been provided?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not get the list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's postpone this until after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I might be able to clear it up. It is exactly the same list that was e-mailed to you of exhibits that would be used with the witness. There is nothing different from the list that was sent out of all the exhibits attached to this witness, including his transcript, which was provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I am against Exhibit 1161, because it is an intercept. So for the time being, I believe this document should not be tendered into evidence. It only should be marked for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You can take that for granted in relation to all intercepts. We'll only mark them for identification purposes. Otherwise, any objections? Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I join the objection raised by my colleague, Madam Fauveau, and also this intercept was also -- only shown to the witness in the course of the cross-examination in the Blagojevic/Jokic case and this was not tendered by the Defence, and the same thing goes for Exhibit 08102 [as interpreted], that's a letter by a member of the Ministry of the Interior. It's addressed to a totally different person, so this witness had no knowledge of it and he did not participate in the drafting of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, it's -- 0082 and 1161 were used by the witness, or were used with the witness during his previous testimony. That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And that's why they were offered. They were used in cross-examination of his previous testimony by Mr. -- well, it doesn't matter, but they were used. If the Court's going to follow the testimony, I think it's important to have them. They're not something I would have put in, in my direct, and I didn't. But they are part of the record, and that's the practice we've been using. The intercept in question will be marked for identification and has been dealt with otherwise, anyway, and the letter was used, questions were put to the witness based on this letter, so I honestly don't understand the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have seen the transcript. Any objections? Yes -- no, no, that is a mistake. In line 24 of the previous page, page 37, it's Exhibit 08102, I take it you were referring to 0082.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood you, because that is the letter from --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honours, correct. And another sentence in relation to intercept 161 [as interpreted]. This intercept was perhaps relevant in the Blagojevic/Jokic case. This witness did not participate in this intercept. I mean the witness who was here today. Now, it was General Zivanovic and Major Jokic who were participants in that intercepts -- in that intercept and I believe that intercept is not relevant for us in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is part and parcel of the testimony of the witness in the previous case, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As we have stated on several previous occasions, the questions of relevance will be dealt with later on, and the transcript of his previous testimony would not be intelligible in the absence of these documents. Still the intercept, of course, will be marked for identification. Any further objections? We hear none. So the rest is admitted. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before we go for the break I would like to return to what I said just before the beginning of the testimony of this witness. And I take this opportunity to apologise to my colleagues from the Prosecution. I've just been shown a second e-mail which I missed in which we were given information that these documents were uploaded into e-court. So I apologise to my colleagues from the Prosecution. Sorry. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can close that chapter, and move ahead. So we will have a 25-minute break and then we will start the -- with witness -- the testimony of Witness number 86, who I hope has been advised that we won't finish with him today. Or very unlikely that we will do. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, you are required to make an undertaking, take -- make an undertaking with us that you will be testifying the truth. Miss -- Madam Usher is going to hand to you the text of the solemn declaration. Please stand up, read it out aloud, and that will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Before you start giving evidence, I wanted to confirm to you that we have, at the request of the Prosecution, put in place for you two protective measures, namely the use of a pseudonym instead of your name, and you will be given a number, and also facial distortion. I suppose these have been explained to you. I just want to have a confirmation from you that you are happy with these -- with this arrangement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't suppose we will finish with your testimony today. We will make an effort. If we don't, we will then continue on Monday. Mr. Thayer will go first with his examination-in-chief. And then he will be followed by the various Defence teams. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning to you, and Your Honours. Good morning everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think a warning from the Bench with respect to this witness would be appropriate, given our past practise, before we go any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection to the use of the word "warning," Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If the Prosecution feels it needs to warn its own witnesses, none, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Witness, you would have certainly followed what Mr. Thayer has just stated. In the experience of this Tribunal sometimes questions are put to witnesses which, if answered, could possibly at least in the mind of the witness himself, or herself, expose him or her to criminal proceedings. We have a Rule that seeks to protect witnesses from incriminating themselves, which is one of the principles enshrined in our Statutes and our Rules. So if, at any time, questions are put to you which, in your opinion, if answered, would -- could possibly expose you to criminal proceedings, then you may object to answer such questions; however, this is not an absolute right. You may object. You may ask us, in other words, to exempt you from answering the question, but we may decide that it is in the interests of justice to compel you to give -- to answer such questions. If we do compel you to answer such questions, then you have a guarantee, according to our law, or Rules, that any testimony that you would be giving because you are compelled to, shall not be used as evidence in any subsequent prosecution against you for any offence, except if you are prosecuted for false testimony, for perjury. Is that clear? Do you require further explanation from me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not require any additional explanations. It is clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, sir. Mr. Thayer will go first, as I have already explained. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, good morning to you. You are being handed a piece of --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You're being handed a piece of paper, and I would just ask you to read it to yourself and if you would, confirm that your name is written on that paper beside the pseudonym PW-160.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And for the record, the pseudonym sheet is P02473.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And although you have not indicated this, this will be kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if we may move into private session for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's move into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I would just like to ask you a couple of questions to help explain a little bit about the structure of the special police brigade. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber, please, how was it organised and structured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: The special police brigade had headquarters in Ilajnik [phoen]. It had nine detachments deployed throughout the Republika Srpska, it had a training centre at Jahorina, and a unit of police dogs, and I don't remember where it was headquartered. I think that within the headquarters there existed also a mixed anti-armour artillery battalion, but it was attached to the headquarters, to the command. That was the structure of the special police brigade, how it was organised. The detachments were deployed to Trebinje, Foca, Jahorina, Sekovici, Janja, Doboj, Banja Luka, and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just two quick follow-up questions, sir. The -- I see the transcript didn't catch the location of the headquarters. If you would, would you just please restate where the headquarters were located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: The detachments were deployed to Trebinje, Foca, Jahorina, Sekovici, Janja, Doboj, Banja Luka, and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wasn't clear in my question. You mentioned the actual headquarters of the special police brigade itself. I don't think the transcript caught it. Can you just restate the location of the actual headquarters of the entire brigade? Where was that located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: The headquarters was located in Janja, which is a village near Bijeljina, some 12 kilometres from Bijeljina. It was in a settlement of weekend cottages in a motel near the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And the detachments that you just described, Janja, Doboj, Sekovici, were those the actual bases of those detachments or where they were billeted? Just so the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: They were actually located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, just briefly, sir, can you tell the Trial Chamber what the basic function of the special police brigade was during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: It was a combat brigade during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, was there a difference between the Jahorina members who were being trained in the summer of 1995 and the regular special brigade members from these various detachments that you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: Yes. There was a difference. On the one hand we had regular members who had experienced some combat action, whereas the other ones had been captured as deserters. They fled from their positions, and then they were deployed to Jahorina to the training centre there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has previously heard reference to units of the special police brigade as opposed to units of what are referred to as the PJP or separate police. Can you just explain the difference as simply as you can?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: Well, the difference is in that the special police brigade was a combat unit, and it mostly was assigned combat assignments. As for the PJP units, they were regular police forces which belonged to public security centres, and they performed police duties at the public security stations and police stations, they were organised in companies, and they also had reserve forces within those companies. I don't know exactly how many companies each centre had.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a little while ago a Mr. Saric. Can you tell the Trial Chamber to whom Mr. Saric reported?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: Deputy minister and minister were his superiors. Minister of the interior. If the minister was absent, then deputy minister was his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in July of 1995, sir, do you know the names of those two people, the minister and deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: I know that the minister came from Novi Grad, I don't remember his name. Or perhaps he was from Bosanski Novi. As for the deputy minister, it was Mr. Tomo Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention now to July of 1995. Do you know approximately when the deserters arrived for training at the Jahorina facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I think that it was a couple of months before the events in the Srebrenica area. Some two and a half to three months prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what type of formations were they organised into?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: They were organised in two companies. The companies had platoons. As far as I remember, they had two or three platoons. I think three platoons each. They numbered some 200-odd men.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is that total therefore 100 men per company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did each company have a commander, sir? And if so, who were those commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: Companies had komandirs or commanders. The commander of the first company was Djuric Mendeljejev, and the second one was commanded by Dzedzo [phoen] Ikonic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At some point in early July 1995, sir, did you receive an order concern ago company of the Jahorina training centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, Mr. Borovcanin came to Jahorina telling us that we had been issued an order to go to Bratunac, that a company was supposed to go to execute assignments there, and that I had to be in Bratunac by 1500 hours, and that I would receive further orders there. I think that he even showed me the order issued by Mr. Tomislav Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we may have 65 ter number 94 displayed on e-court, please. Just asking you if you see a document on your screen, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recognise what that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: This is the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you would, sir, would you just read paragraphs 2 and 3 aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just 2 and 3 is fine, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: "The second special detachment of police from Sekovici, the 1st Company of PJP of the public security centre in Zvornik mixed company of joint forces of the MUP of Republika Srpska --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of the RSK, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "-- of Serbia and Republika Srpska and a company from the training centre in Jahorina are to become part of the unit." Item 3, "I designate Ljubisa Borovcanin, deputy commander of the special police brigade, as the commander of the MUP unit."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you see, sir, who issued this order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: The staff commander, Tomislav Kovac. It says here, "staff commander, Tomislav Kovac." I know that at the time Mr. Kovac was deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may just scroll up a bit, please, Madam Usher. And do you see a date on this order, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: 10th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what, if anything, you did as a result of receiving this order from Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: The company got ready, and we travelled to Bratunac. In Bratunac we got in touch with Mr. Borovcanin, and we were told that we were to be housed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection to the form of the question. Because it says here when you received the order from Mr. Borovcanin, and in his previous answer the witness indicated that this order had been issued by Mr. Tomislav Kovac. So this could actually mislead us all in terms of who actually issued this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can see it clear enough, Tomislav Kovac had issued the order that was shown to the witness by -- according to him, Ljubomir Borovcanin, who ordered him to report as he testified before. So we have got two orders. One to Borovcanin and one to the witness. The one to the witness is from Borovcanin according to him, and not directly from, so I think it's clear enough. We can proceed, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you were answering the question, what if anything you did as a result of receiving the order from Mr. Borovcanin. And you had just said that you had -- "we had gotten in touch with Mr. Borovcanin upon arrival in Bratunac."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: Yes, we were given an order to -- that we were to be billeted in the village of Bilosevac, I don't remember the exact name of the village, in a school when we got there, I think that our quarters were already ready, and then we were -- I was supposed to await further orders there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let me just stop you right there, sir, and ask a couple of follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could ask him to repeat the name of the village because it doesn't show up in the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to the village where you were accommodated. Could you restate the name as you remember it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-160
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was Bjelosevac or Bjelovac. Something like. I can't really recall the name anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can I tell the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
